title: If you declare a local variable inside `main()` but do not initialize it and then try to print it, what happens and why?
shortTitle: If you declare a local variable in main but do not initialize it and print it, what happens

s1_definition.profdef: The code does not compile. Unlike instance and static fields, local variables in Java are never given a default value, and the compiler enforces definite assignment, which means every local variable must be provably assigned a value along every path that reaches a point where it is read. Attempting to print an uninitialized local produces the compile-time error "variable might not have been initialized." This is a deliberate language safety rule, not a runtime failure: the program never even starts, because the compiler refuses to produce bytecode that would read a local whose value is undefined. The fix is to assign the variable before any read, either at declaration or on every path leading to the read.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a local variable is like a figure a teller jots on a scrap pad while serving one customer, and that scrap pad is blank and personal, not a pre-printed form. The bank has a strict rule that a teller may never read a number off the scrap pad unless they can prove they actually wrote it there first, because a stray number could cause a wrong transaction. So if a teller tries to read a figure they never wrote, the bank's auditor stops the whole transaction before it starts and refuses to let it proceed, which is the compiler refusing to compile. This is different from the pre-printed passbook fields, meaning instance variables, which come with a safe default of zero already printed.
s1_definition.oneliner: It will not compile, because local variables get no default and Java's definite-assignment rule forbids reading a local that has not provably been assigned on every path to the read.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The code does not compile. Unlike instance and static fields, local variables in Java are never given a default value, and the compiler enforces definite assignment, which means every local variable must be provably assigned a value along every path that reaches a point where it is read. Attempting to print an uninitialized local produces the compile-time error "variable might not have been initialized." This is a deliberate language safety rule, not a runtime failure: the program never even starts, because the compiler refuses to produce bytecode that would read a local whose value is undefined. The fix is to assign the variable before any read, either at declaration or on every path leading to the read.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a local variable is like a figure a teller jots on a scrap pad while serving one customer, and that scrap pad is blank and personal, not a pre-printed form. The bank has a strict rule that a teller may never read a number off the scrap pad unless they can prove they actually wrote it there first, because a stray number could cause a wrong transaction. So if a teller tries to read a figure they never wrote, the bank's auditor stops the whole transaction before it starts and refuses to let it proceed, which is the compiler refusing to compile. This is different from the pre-printed passbook fields, meaning instance variables, which come with a safe default of zero already printed.

**One line to remember:** It will not compile, because local variables get no default and Java's definite-assignment rule forbids reading a local that has not provably been assigned on every path to the read.

sections.s2_technical:
The core rule is definite assignment, specified in the Java Language Specification. For a local variable, the compiler must be able to prove that the variable has been assigned a value before every use. If there is any path through the method where the variable is read without having been assigned, compilation fails with "variable might not have been initialized." So `int balance; System.out.println(balance);` fails because balance is read on a path where it was never assigned.

This is intentionally stricter than fields. Instance and static fields receive automatic defaults, so an unset int field reads zero. Local variables deliberately do not, because the language designers decided that reading an accidentally-unset local is almost always a bug, and catching it at compile time is far safer than silently using zero. The result is that the error surfaces immediately at build time rather than as a wrong value at runtime.

The analysis is path-sensitive, not merely a check for a single assignment line. The compiler considers all branches. For example `int fee; if (amount > 1000) fee = 20; System.out.println(fee);` still fails, because on the path where amount is not greater than one thousand, fee was never assigned. To satisfy the rule you must assign on every path: add an else that assigns fee, or initialize fee at declaration. Conversely `int fee; if (amount > 1000) fee = 20; else fee = 0; System.out.println(fee);` compiles, because both branches assign before the read.

The rule interacts with control flow in subtle ways. If a branch definitely throws or returns, the compiler treats paths after it as unreachable for the variable, so `int fee; if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); else fee = amount; use(fee);` compiles because the only surviving path assigns fee. A variable assigned inside a loop that might execute zero times is not considered definitely assigned afterward, so the compiler still complains.

Several senior points matter. First, this rule is exactly why a final local can be assigned later as long as it is assigned exactly once on every path before use, enabling the common pattern of a final variable set in both branches of an if. Second, it explains a frequent beginner confusion: fields appear to work uninitialized while locals do not, and the explanation is defaults for fields versus definite assignment for locals. Third, in banking code this rule is a quiet ally, because it prevents a transfer method from ever reading an unset fee or amount and silently moving the wrong money; the build fails first. The correct habit is to initialize locals at declaration when a sensible default exists, or to ensure every branch assigns before the read, which also makes the code's intent explicit.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A developer declared a local fee inside a transfer routine and printed it before assigning, and the project would not build at all. This is exactly the definite-assignment rule rejecting an uninitialized local read.

Problem 2 — Another developer assigned the fee only inside an if branch, so one path left it unset, and the build still failed. This is exactly the path-sensitive nature of definite assignment.

Problem 3 — The correct version assigns the fee on every path, either by initializing at declaration or by covering both branches, and the build succeeds and prints the right value. This is exactly how to satisfy the rule.

Because an uninitialized read does not compile, the runnable demo shows the compiling, correct version and documents the broken versions as commented-out code with the exact compiler error, inside a `LocalVariableDemo` main class that computes a transfer fee for Rajesh.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile (succeeds because all locals are definitely assigned)
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/core/LocalVariableDemo.java

# If you UNCOMMENT a BROKEN block, javac fails with, for example:
#   LocalVariableDemo.java:XX: error: variable fee might not have been initialized

# Run
java -cp out com.bank.core.LocalVariableDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer amount of fifty thousand rupees for Rajesh, used to decide a fee.

Step 1 — The amount is a local reference assigned immediately, so it is definitely assigned and safe to read. The broken examples are kept commented out because if they were active the compiler would reject the entire file before any bytecode is produced.

Step 2 — In the first correct version, the fee local is initialized to zero at its declaration. This guarantees it has a value on every path, so even if the if does not run, the fee is a safe zero. The compiler is satisfied because the variable is definitely assigned.

Step 3 — In the second correct version, the fee local is declared without a value, but both branches of the if assign it: twenty for a high-value transfer and zero for a small one. Because every path assigns before the read, the compiler proves definite assignment and allows the print.

Step 4 — In the third correct version, one branch throws an exception rather than assigning. The compiler recognizes that the throwing path never reaches the read, so the only surviving path, the else, assigns the fee, which satisfies definite assignment.

Step 5 — Because the amount is fifty thousand, which exceeds one thousand, each correct version computes a fee of twenty, and the program prints all three fees and a confirmation. No runtime default was ever involved; correctness was enforced entirely at compile time.

```
Oct 30, 2026 4:44:22 PM com.bank.core.LocalVariableDemo main
INFO: Fee via declaration-init = 20
INFO: Fee via every-path assignment = 20
INFO: Fee via guard-then-assign = 20
INFO: All locals were definitely assigned before use → compiles and runs.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Compiler: definite-assignment analysis BEFORE any bytecode
    │
    ├─ int fee; print(fee)                → path with NO assignment → COMPILE ERROR ✗
    │
    ├─ int fee; if(cond) fee=20; print    → else path unassigned     → COMPILE ERROR ✗
    │
    ├─ int fee=0; if(cond) fee=20; print  → always assigned          → OK ✓
    │
    ├─ int fee; if(cond) fee=20; else fee=0; print → every path set  → OK ✓
    │
    └─ int fee; if(bad) throw; else fee=20; use    → survivor set    → OK ✓
         │
         ▼
   only if ALL paths assign before read → javac emits class → runs
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Definite Assignment for Locals ═══

  ┌─ Key Rules ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Locals get NO default (unlike fields which default to 0/null)     │
  │  Compiler proves: assigned on EVERY path before each read          │
  │  Partial assignment (one branch only) → error                      │
  │  Throw/return branch → path pruned from analysis                   │
  │  Loop that may run 0× → not definitely assigned after              │
  │  Error: "variable X might not have been initialized"               │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: fee computation isolated; each path assigns one clear value    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── State: variable assignment status (compiler view) ──────

  [DECLARED, UNASSIGNED]
      │ read here → COMPILE ERROR
      ▼ assign on a path
  [ASSIGNED ON SOME PATHS]
      │ read here → ERROR if any path still unassigned
      ▼ assign on ALL paths (or prune via throw/return)
  [DEFINITELY ASSIGNED] → read allowed → compiles

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. amount = 50000 (definitely assigned reference)
  2. feeInitialized = 0 at declaration → safe
  3. if(amount>1000) feeInitialized = 20
  4. feeEveryPath: both branches assign → OK
  5. feeGuarded: throw branch pruned, else assigns → OK
  6. print all three → 20, 20, 20
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
If I declare a local variable inside main and try to print it without assigning it, the code does not compile at all, and the compiler reports that the variable might not have been initialized. The reason is that local variables in Java never receive a default value, unlike instance and static fields which default to zero, false, or null. Instead the language enforces a rule called definite assignment, which requires the compiler to prove that every local has been assigned a value along every path that reaches a point where it is read.

This is a deliberate safety decision, not a runtime accident. The designers decided that reading an accidentally unset local is almost always a bug, so instead of silently substituting zero, the compiler refuses to produce any bytecode and the program never starts. That is a much safer outcome than discovering a wrong value at runtime, and in a bank it is a genuine ally, because it makes it impossible for a transfer method to read an unset fee or amount and silently move the wrong money; the build simply fails first.

The analysis is path-sensitive, which trips people up. It is not enough to assign the variable somewhere; it must be assigned on every path that leads to the read. So assigning a fee only inside an if branch still fails to compile, because the else path leaves it unassigned. To satisfy the rule I either initialize the local at its declaration with a sensible default, or I make sure every branch assigns it before the read. The compiler is also smart about control flow: if a branch definitely throws or returns, it prunes that path, so a guard that throws on an invalid amount and otherwise assigns the fee compiles, because the only surviving path does assign.

The senior points I add are that this same mechanism is what lets a final local be assigned exactly once later, as long as it is assigned on every path before use, which is a clean pattern for setting a value in both branches of an if. It also cleanly explains the common beginner confusion about why fields seem to work uninitialized while locals do not, and the answer is defaults for fields versus definite assignment for locals. My habit in banking code is to initialize locals at declaration when a sensible default exists and otherwise to ensure every branch assigns before any read, which both satisfies the compiler and makes the intent of the code obvious to the next reader.
